title: Five years: the stories
hookLine: the Gurus, the sakhis, the martyrs and the tellers
tomorrow: Maya has never eaten langar. what will she notice first?

cards: Two minutes is nothing on a video app and forever at a microphone. Simran timed it: that's what each senior gets at the send-off. Her notes app has a list longer than two minutes could ever hold.
Nanak at the river. Bhai Lalo's bread. The ninth Guru who stood up for other people's faith.
Bebe's stories from the stove. She has to pick one.

teach.b: Sikhs carry a lot of their faith in stories. There are the Gurus' lives. There are sakhis, the stories told about them, often collected in the janamsakhis about Guru Nanak, and versions differ.

There are the martyrs, like Guru Tegh Bahadur, remembered for standing up for other people's freedom to believe. And there are the tellers: dhadi singers, speakers at the gurdwara, grandmothers at the stove.

teach.h: A SAKHI IS TOLD FOR ITS POINT.
teach.b: A sakhi is told for its point. Take Bhai Lalo. Tradition says Guru Nanak stayed with Lalo, a carpenter, and turned down the feast of Malik Bhago, a rich official.

When the Guru squeezed the two breads, the story says, Lalo's dripped milk and Bhago's dripped blood. Nobody tells that one for the chemistry. It's about honest work and food earned off other people's backs.
Simran scrolls the list again and lands on one she didn't expect. Tradition says Guru Nanak didn't travel alone.
Beside him walked Bhai Mardana, a Muslim musician, playing the rebab while the Guru sang.
Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: the first Guru's hymns were carried on the road by a Muslim friend's music. Maya will be at the send-off. Simran picks the two friends on the road.

how: Sikh stories are told in katha at the gurdwara, sung by dhadi singers, read from collections of sakhis and retold at home; many children first hear the Gurus' lives from a parent or grandparent.

games.q: who's who in the stories — tap the pairs.

s: the sakhis are word-for-word records, the same in every telling
they're stories tradition tells and retells, and versions differ. they're told for their point.
tradition says Guru Nanak traveled with Bhai Mardana, a Muslim musician
Mardana played the rebab while the Guru sang.
in the Bhai Lalo story, Nanak chooses the rich man's feast
he stays with Lalo, the carpenter, and turns the feast down.

games.q: your uncle retells the Bhai Lalo story at dinner, and your little cousin asks, did the bread really drip milk?
o: it's a sakhi: tradition tells it that way, and its point is honest work.
yes, every detail was written down the day it happened, exactly.
no, so it's just a made-up story and doesn't really count.
games.why: a sakhi is told for its point. Lalo's bread and Bhago's feast are about food earned honestly and food taken off others' backs.

practice: Pick the story you'd tell if you had two minutes, a Sikh one you've met here or any story that stayed with you. Tell it out loud, quietly, to the room: who, what happened, and the one thing it means to you.
If you finish early, tell it again, shorter.

wordCard.voice: Five years: the stories. A look back at the Gurus, the sakhis, the martyrs, and everyone who kept telling them.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a story from the Gurus' lives, told and retold for what it teaches.

carryVoice: Your line: the stories, told again so they stay alive. Two friends on a road, and two minutes to tell it.
